![](images/c7/c7b322970113e415b78a9cc74469c6cad86404f0929e2091f8c6be2e1329f7bf.svg)" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A\left(A^T\!A\right)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^3.$ In our case, we have
![](images/73/736da2e7e8541700ba158e3b983bc2320427755eb7da3190b62dc743972d083c.svg)
Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 & 2 \\ -2 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 & 2 \\ -2 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}12 & 4 \\ 4 & 12\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}12 \\ -20\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{32}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}12 \\ -20\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133597 :question/problem "Verify whether the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$ are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the vectors $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3 \},$ where
![](images/e1/e11a1239e429520c575fed6ac0c9af383ba8ce58b6df8616218998a58c63748c.svg)" :question/worked-solution "First, we verify whether $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-4){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & -2 & -10 \\ 0 & -3 & -15\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{3}{2}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & -2 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.
$$

In our case, we have
![](images/78/7885074c85f490a410f26a1b4d7836134b13a36923b99d31e3b670b8c1dd75f5.svg)

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}26 & 8 \\ 8 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}18 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{14}[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ -8 & 26\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}18 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135049 :tutorial/content "We've already seen how to find the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace in the case when the subspace is defined using an orthogonal basis. In this lesson, we'll learn how to do the same thing in the case of non-orthogonal bases.

For example, consider the following vectors:
![](images/28/28ce7470231775d8889555d0dd9f37ee9215044762a40335bd43578b121486a3.svg)
How can we find the orthogonal projection $\mathbf{x}_S$ of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}?$ Notice that since $\mathbf a_1\cdot \mathbf a_2 \neq 0,$ the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ are not orthogonal.

As usual, we would like to write $\mathbf{x}$ as 

$$
\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_S + \mathbf{x}_{S^\perp},
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \mathbf{a}_2 \in S$ and $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \!\in S^\perp.$

![](images/3a/3a5576fcaf9e0be6fc14978eb91dcbaceee75cbfddaa537fdb05d34b8e31e2e0.png)

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}} & =x-{x}_{S} \\  & =x-({k}_{1}{a}_{1}+{k}_{2}{a}_{2}) \\  & =x-{k}_{1}{a}_{1}-{k}_{2}{a}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \in S^\perp,$ that is, $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \perp S,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{1} \\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{2}\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the expression for $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp}$ into the system to get
![](images/f1/f1e3c7ae9e966ebcab88901c9e44a5449cb98716f43fc526d306e0af5186923b.svg)

We can write this system in an equivalent matrix form as follows:
![](images/47/472c41e1e509d2db9c41dfa95127382eeba7ab5fbaa4172d680c39335694ef2e.svg)

If we denote 
![](images/26/2650c1020d413a7c988279cc698ab4b7c4caff427615d49b35ef4e9a42651ff0.svg)
and ![](images/9b/9b50884bd0af404e71f9d7734e9bc054fc9439aba02780cf2beb5fa0a6ac1f32.svg) then we obtain

$$
A^TA\mathbf{k} = A^T\mathbf{x}
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	\mathbf{k}=(A^TA)^{-1}A^T\mathbf{x}.
$$

Also, we note that  $\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \mathbf{a}_2$ can be expressed as $\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x}	= A\mathbf{k}.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =Ak \\  & =A({A}^{T}A)^{-1}{A}^{T}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a formula for the orthogonal projection!

Now, we return to our example. Using the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}6 & 8 \\ 8 & 11\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}11 & -8 \\ -8 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Note**: Pay attention to the order in which we carried out the multiplication. Carrying out the operations in the order shown above can save us a lot of work!" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135050 :tutorial/content "If $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$ is a set of *linearly independent* vectors, then the orthogonal projection of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S = \textrm{span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x},
$$

 
where $A$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n,$ that is,
![](images/25/25a85721a3721ace1a32f6ed457749091452df93053d2eba7dbfaa48f6f74189.svg)

**Watch out!** The fact that $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$ must be linearly independent is important. If the vectors are linearly dependent, we need to find the basis of the span before applying the formula." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135051 :tutorial/content "As we've already seen, the orthogonal projection of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the one-dimensional subspace $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ is given by 

$$
\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{a}} \, \mathbf{x} = \dfrac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a}} \: \mathbf{a}.
$$

If we suppose that $\mathbf{a}$ denotes the column-vector ![](images/c2/c23a26d5ce1137e222e28a4bc872f9bcffda2cd6430f2d5532618ccf0ed95fa5.svg) then the dot product $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a}$ is simply $\mathbf{a}^T \mathbf{a},$ and we can write the formula as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{(a\cdot x)}{(a\cdot a)}\,a \\  & =[\frac{({a}^{T}x)}{({a}^{T}a)}]a \\  & =a[\frac{({a}^{T}x)}{({a}^{T}a)}] \\  & =a[({a}^{T}a)^{-1}{a}^{T}x] \\  & =a\,({a}^{T}a)^{-1}{a}^{T}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's compare the above with the formula that we use when we want to project onto an arbitrary subspace:

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}
$$

 
As we can see, they are basically the same thing!" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134003 :activity/expected-seconds 1020.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

using an orthogonal basis. In this lesson, we'll learn how to do the same thing in the case of non-orthogonal bases.

For example, consider the following vectors:

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

How can we find the orthogonal projection $\mathbf{x}_S$ of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}?$ Notice that since $\mathbf a_1\cdot \mathbf a_2 \neq 0,$ the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ are not orthogonal.

As usual, we would like to write $\mathbf{x}$ as 

$$
\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_S + \mathbf{x}_{S^\perp},
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \mathbf{a}_2 \in S$ and $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \!\in S^\perp.$

![](images/3a/3a5576fcaf9e0be6fc14978eb91dcbaceee75cbfddaa537fdb05d34b8e31e2e0.png)

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}} & =x-{x}_{S} \\  & =x-({k}_{1}{a}_{1}+{k}_{2}{a}_{2}) \\  & =x-{k}_{1}{a}_{1}-{k}_{2}{a}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \in S^\perp,$ that is, $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \perp S,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{1} \\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{2}\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the expression for $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp}$ into the system to get

$$
{\begin{aligned}(x-{k}_{1}{a}_{1}-{k}_{2}{a}_{2})\cdot {a}_{1}=0 \\ (x-{k}_{1}{a}_{1}-{k}_{2}{a}_{2})\cdot {a}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

We can write this system in an equivalent matrix form as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\,\,{a}_{1}\,\,- \\ -\,\,{a}_{2}\,\,-\end{aligned}]
$$

If we denote 
$[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]$
and $[\begin{aligned}{k}_{1} \\ {k}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ then we obtain

$$
A^TA\mathbf{k} = A^T\mathbf{x}
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	\mathbf{k}=(A^TA)^{-1}A^T\mathbf{x}.
$$

Also, we note that  $\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \mathbf{a}_2$ can be expressed as $\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x}	= A\mathbf{k}.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =Ak \\  & =A({A}^{T}A)^{-1}{A}^{T}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a formula for the orthogonal projection!

Now, we return to our example. Using the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}6 & 8 \\ 8 & 11\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}11 & -8 \\ -8 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Note**: Pay attention to the order in which we carried out the multiplication. Carrying out the operations in the order shown above can save us a lot of work!" :tutorial/id #uuid "0a9a954f-9338-5c3f-a9db-9b39a1a60c0b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3626 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "f3cce71c-fd0d-5040-949b-813f3fdcbdd7" :step/math-academy-id 20246 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134676}} {:db/id 17592186134675 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133788 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133597 :question/id #uuid "b8bbe0e1-8bf1-5b3a-a77e-6350ea77e83f" :question/math-academy-id "e-5575"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ad9f55b2-ce37-507f-8cb6-7d4e30e6868a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134296} {:db/id 17592186134301} {:db/id 17592186272103} {:db/id 17592186275452} {:db/id 17592186326787} {:db/id 17592186326854} {:db/id 17592186366111} {:db/id 17592186382580} {:db/id 17592186388723} {:db/id 17592186388960} {:db/id 17592186388967} {:db/id 17592186388974} {:db/id 17592186392354}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace"} :step/id #uuid "8e0f305d-efdf-586e-b799-66fe2b5a8f6a" :step/math-academy-id 20247 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134678}} {:db/id 17592186134676 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135050 :tutorial/content "If $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$ is a set of *linearly independent* vectors, then the orthogonal projection of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S = \textrm{span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{(a\cdot x)}{(a\cdot a)}\,a \\  & =[\frac{({a}^{T}x)}{({a}^{T}a)}]a \\  & =a[\frac{({a}^{T}x)}{({a}^{T}a)}] \\  & =a[({a}^{T}a)^{-1}{a}^{T}x] \\  & =a\,({a}^{T}a)^{-1}{a}^{T}x.\end{aligned}

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}
$$
